title: IEEE 2863-2026, Organizational Governance of AI
subtitle: IEEE's recommended practice for how a governing body directs and oversees AI
body_html:
On this page

  • What IEEE 2863 is
  • What it is not: a certificate
  • How it got here: the IEEE record
  • What it addresses, from IEEE's public record
  • How it relates to the other frameworks
  • How to put IEEE 2863 to work: a 5-step path
  • Frequently asked questions about IEEE 2863
  • How this page was written
  • Primary sources on IEEE 2863

The one-paragraph answer

IEEE 2863-2026, the IEEE Recommended Practice for Organizational Governance of Artificial Intelligence, is an IEEE standard published on 16 October 2026 that sets out what the governing body of an organisation that develops or uses AI should do to make that use responsible, ethical and accountable. It gives governance principles for the board to consider and prioritise, processes for putting them into effect, and case studies on resolving tensions between the principles. It is a recommended practice, not a requirements standard, so no organisation can be certified to it. It comes from the IEEE Computer Society's Artificial Intelligence Standards Committee.

What IEEE 2863 is

IEEE publishes three kinds of standards documents: standards, which state requirements with "shall"; recommended practices, which state preferred procedures with "should"; and guides. IEEE 2863-2026 is the second kind. Its subject is the top of the organisation: the board of directors or equivalent governing body, and what it should expect of management when the organisation builds or uses AI.

IEEE's abstract describes three parts: a set of governance principles that the organisation's governing body should consider and prioritise; a set of processes the governing body should consider to implement those principles; and a series of case studies involving specific AI applications that show how the processes are used, including how to resolve tensions between principles.

The project was run by the IEEE working group AI Governance, Organizational Governance of Artificial Intelligence, chaired by Gary Marchant, under the Computer Society's Artificial Intelligence Standards Committee (C/AISC).

What it is not: a certificate

A recommended practice says what an organisation should do, not what it shall do, so there is nothing in it for a certification body to audit against. There is no IEEE 2863 certificate, and a supplier that claims one is describing something that does not exist. What an organisation can honestly say is that its board's approach to AI governance took IEEE 2863 into account.

Where a certificate is wanted, the AI management system standard is ISO/IEC 42001. The two answer different questions: 42001 asks whether the organisation runs an auditable AI management system, and IEEE 2863 asks how the governing body directs and oversees AI in the first place. Our AI Assurance Standards page covers how to read each kind of assurance claim.

How it got here: the IEEE record

The dates below are from the standard's page on the IEEE Standards Association site, read on 24 October 2026.

DateStep
2020-02-13Project Authorization Request (PAR) approved, opening project P2863
2026-06-04Approved by the IEEE SA Standards Board
2026-10-16Published as IEEE 2863-2026; status Active Standard

Publication came six and a half years after authorisation, a span that covers the arrival of generative AI. Commentary written while the project was still P2863 describes drafts, not the published text.

What it addresses, from IEEE's public record

The keywords IEEE lists for the standard give the clearest public view of its scope: accountability, auditing, competency, controllability, effectiveness, ethics oversight, explainability, governance, human oversight, incident response, intellectual property assessment, life cycle oversight, non-discrimination, privacy, red teaming, safety, security, social balance, stakeholder identification and engagement, stewardship and environmental sustainability, transparency, trustworthiness, value chain management and well-being.

Read as a list, that is close to the full set of topics a board is asked about when AI goes wrong: who was accountable, whether anyone could have intervened, whether the system was tested adversarially, whether there was an incident plan, and what the organisation's suppliers were doing. It is a list of keywords, not the standard's structure; for how the standard treats each one, read it.

How IEEE 2863 relates to the other frameworks

We have found no formal mapping between IEEE 2863 and any of the frameworks below, from IEEE or from their publishers. The comparisons are ours, made from each framework's public material.

Director oversight duties

In the United States the board's legal duty comes from case law, not from a standard: the Caremark line of Delaware cases requires directors to make a good-faith effort to put a reporting system in place for material risks and to respond to red flags. Our Director Oversight page and the Board Advisory and Fiduciary Risk section cover what that duty asks of a board when AI is material. IEEE 2863 is a published reference a board can point to when it describes how it set up that oversight. Following it is not a legal safe harbour.

ISO/IEC 42001, the AI management system

ISO/IEC 42001:2023 is the certifiable management system standard: leadership, AI risk assessment and treatment, controls, internal audit and improvement. Its leadership clause expects top management to commit to the system. IEEE 2863 sits one level above, at the governing body that sets direction and holds management to account. A board that has adopted IEEE 2863's principles will usually rely on a 42001 system, or something like it, to put them into practice.

The NIST AI RMF

The NIST AI Risk Management Framework (NIST AI 100-1, January 2023) is a voluntary US framework whose Govern function covers policies, accountability structures, culture and oversight across the organisation. IEEE 2863 addresses similar ground from the board's chair rather than the risk function's, and adds case studies on trade-offs between principles, which the RMF leaves to its users.

ISO/IEC 38507

ISO/IEC 38507:2022 is the international guidance on the governance implications of AI for organisations, written for governing bodies in the ISO/IEC 38500 IT governance family. It is the closest international counterpart to IEEE 2863 in audience. Both are guidance, so the choice between them is about which vocabulary an organisation already uses.

The EU AI Act

The EU AI Act places obligations on providers and deployers, not on boards as such, and it gives a presumption of conformity only to harmonised European standards cited in the Official Journal, such as EN 18286. IEEE 2863 is not one, and following it gives no presumption under the Act. It can still shape the accountability framework that Article 17(1)(m) asks a provider's quality management system to set out.

How to put IEEE 2863 to work: a 5-step path

These steps are our own practical sequence for a board secretary or general counsel who has just heard of the standard. They are not drawn from the standard's text.

  1. Get a copy for the governing body. IEEE sells the standard, and its page also points to the IEEE GET Program, through which IEEE makes some standards available without charge. This page does not summarise the standard and cannot stand in for it.
  2. Decide where AI sits on the board's agenda. Name the committee that owns AI oversight, how often it hears about AI, and what management must bring to it. Write it into the committee's charter.
  3. Agree the principles and their order. The standard asks the governing body to consider and prioritise principles. Doing that explicitly, before a dispute, is what lets the board resolve a clash between them later.
  4. Tie the principles to a management system. Ask management to show how the board's principles appear in an ISO/IEC 42001 system, the NIST AI RMF or the organisation's existing risk framework, with named owners.
  5. Test it on a real case. Walk the board through one of the organisation's own AI systems, or an incident elsewhere, the way the standard's case studies do, and minute what the board would have needed to know and when.

Frequently asked questions about IEEE 2863

When was IEEE 2863 published?

On 16 October 2026, according to its page on the IEEE SA site. The IEEE SA Standards Board approved it on 4 June 2026, and the project was authorised on 13 February 2020.

Can an organisation be certified to IEEE 2863?

No. It is a recommended practice, not a requirements standard, so there is nothing to certify against. Certification for an AI management system is against ISO/IEC 42001.

Who is it for?

The governing body of any organisation that develops or uses AI, which for most companies means the board of directors, and the executives and advisers who support it.

Is IEEE 2863 the same as P2863?

Yes. P2863 was the project number while it was being drafted; the P is dropped on approval and the year of publication is added.

Does following IEEE 2863 satisfy the EU AI Act or US law?

No. It is a voluntary recommended practice. It gives no presumption of conformity under the EU AI Act and no safe harbour under US law, though it can help a board document how it carries out its oversight.

How does it differ from ISO/IEC 42001?

ISO/IEC 42001 is a certifiable management system run by management. IEEE 2863 is guidance for the governing body that oversees management. Most organisations that take both seriously will use 42001, or something like it, to carry out what the board decides under 2863.

How this page was written

The facts about the standard on this page, its title, status, committee, working group and chair, dates, abstract and keywords, come from the standard's page on the IEEE Standards Association site as our editor read it on 24 October 2026. We have not read the standard itself. This page was drafted with AI assistance from those facts and from the public material of the other frameworks it compares; it does not quote, summarise or paraphrase the standard's clauses, and nothing on it is presented as the standard's wording.
